# Beyond the Frame: A Reading of Identity, Fear, and Fragility

The speaker begins by refusing the narrow image that mainstream media so readily assigns to a young Black man. He is not the figure conjured by sneaker commercials, not the body reduced to athletic spectacle, not the silhouette framed against gritty street imagery for the sake of marketability. This rejection is deliberate and pointed—it insists that his identity cannot be flattened into the commercial and cultural clichés that so often stand in for actual Black personhood.

From this refusal, the text moves outward into a sharper critique of how news outlets handle Black victims of violence. Rather than mourning them as full human beings, coverage frequently pivots to superficial or criminalizing details: commentary on what the victim was wearing, or loaded phrases like "Gang Related" that transform a person into a suspect even in death. Through this lens, the media becomes complicit in a subtle re-victimization, shaping public perception to justify the very violence it reports.

The poem grounds these observations in real-world consequences. It gestures toward "stand your ground" laws and the shootings they have enabled—moments where racial profiling turns ordinary spaces into sites of lethal danger. A store checkout line, a place of unremarkable daily routine, becomes a setting where a Black man's mere presence can be read as threat, where suspicion can escalate into deadly force without accountability.

Confronted with this atmosphere of constant scrutiny, the speaker attempts a strategy of self-protection through appearance. He reaches for the markers of respectability: No Wrinkle Dockers, a navy blazer, an Obama tie. Each item is chosen to signal harmlessness, professionalism, belonging. The goal is a kind of invisibility—to dress in a way that disarms the gaze of those who might otherwise perceive him as dangerous, to move through the world unnoticed and therefore unharmed.

Yet the poem's final image dismantles this hope with devastating clarity. The speaker becomes a dandelion "with his head blown off"—a fragile, common flower, casually destroyed. The image insists that no amount of assimilation, no carefully assembled costume of respectability, can ultimately shield him. Whatever he wears, however he softens his presence, the threat remains. In this closing gesture, the text delivers its hardest truth: that respectability was never a real defense, and that survival cannot be secured simply by making oneself smaller, safer, or more palatable in the eyes of those primed to see a threat.
outputs.L4:
# When Sensible Shoes Can't Save You

They told us how to survive. Pull up your pants. Cut your hair. Speak like you swallowed a dictionary. Dress like you belong in the rooms where decisions get made about lives like yours.

So watch me perform the arithmetic of survival.

*Not the jersey.* Not the number stitched across broad shoulders, not the sweat-slicked promise of a body built for someone else's Saturday entertainment. I fold that image away. It draws too much attention, they say. It makes you *threatening.*

*Not the hoodie.* Not the soft gray cotton pulled against November wind, not the fabric that became a shroud, that turned a boy walking home into a headline, into a hashtag, into a mother's endless midnight. I leave that hanging in the closet. It makes you *suspicious.*

*Not the gold, not the fitted cap, not the bass in the trunk.* Not the swagger they've decided means danger, not the style they've criminalized, not the culture they consume for profit and punish on sight. I strip that away too.

Instead—

Watch me button this oxford shirt. Watch me knot this tie in a mirror, precise as an apology I never owed. Watch me lace up these *sensible* shoes, sensible being the word they use when they mean *acceptable,* when they mean *palatable,* when they mean *less like yourself and more like us.*

Watch me become the exception. The credit to my race. The one they'll say was *articulate,* was *going places,* was *not like the others.*

Watch me disappear into respectability like it's a bunker.

And still.

*And still.*

The bullet doesn't read my résumé. The badge doesn't pause to admire my diction. The finger on the trigger doesn't notice the crease in my slacks, the polish on my shoes, the diploma framed and waiting on some wall I'll never walk past again.

Because the thing they never told us—
the lie folded inside every lesson about survival—
is that the target was never the clothes.

The target was the skin.

You can dress a Black man in every uniform of your comfort. You can teach him to shrink, to smile, to soften every edge until he's more symbol than self. You can make him *sensible.*

And they will kill him sensible.

They will kill him in a suit and call it justified.
They will kill him reaching for his wallet, his phone, his license, his *life,* and call it reasonable fear.

So don't tell me what to wear.
Don't tell me the hoodie killed him.
Don't tell me the music, the walk, the way he wore his youth like armor that turned out to be paper.

Tell me the truth:

There is no fabric thick enough.
There is no costume convincing enough.
There is no version of *acceptable*
that unloads the gun already pointed at my chest.

I am dressed to kill, they said.

They just never told me
*who was holding the weapon.*

# The Colorful World of Sneakers: When Nike Meets Skittles

Sneaker culture has always celebrated bold colors and creative designs, and few combinations capture attention quite like vibrant, candy-inspired trainers. The playful connection between Nike footwear and the rainbow appeal of Skittles represents how brands and colors influence modern fashion.

## A Rainbow on Your Feet

Nike, one of the world's most recognizable athletic brands, has built its reputation on innovation, performance, and eye-catching aesthetics. Over the years, the company has released countless colorful trainer designs that echo the bright, multicolored appeal that Skittles candy is famous for. The phrase "taste the rainbow" could easily apply to some of Nike's most vivid sneaker collections.

## Why Bright Colors Matter

The popularity of colorful trainers stems from several factors:

- **Self-expression**: Vibrant sneakers allow wearers to showcase their personality
- **Nostalgia**: Candy-bright colors evoke fun childhood memories
- **Street style**: Bold footwear has become central to urban fashion
- **Collectibility**: Limited edition colorways drive sneaker enthusiasm

## The Sneaker Community

Trainers have evolved from simple athletic equipment into cultural icons. Enthusiasts, often called "sneakerheads," seek out unique designs featuring striking color palettes. Whether inspired by candy, nature, or pure imagination, colorful Nike trainers continue to dominate the market.

## Conclusion

The intersection of athletic brands like Nike, the playful rainbow appeal reminiscent of Skittles, and the ever-popular trainer market demonstrates how color and creativity shape modern footwear. As long as people love expressing themselves through fashion, brightly colored sneakers will remain a beloved staple.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about a young Black man consciously dressing to avoid being profiled or killed, weaving in brand names, hip-hop references, and biting commentary on media coverage of Black death.
counterfactuals.output:
# Uniform for Staying Alive

*morning inventory, or how to translate a body into something that lives past noon*

—

I select the polo. Ralph Lauren, that little man on horseback riding toward whiteness, riding toward *he seemed like a good kid*. I button it to the throat like closing a case file before it opens. Khakis, pressed. Dockers. I am dressing for the courtroom of the sidewalk, where the verdict comes at 900 feet per second.

No hoodie. Trayvon taught the fabric a new definition. Now cotton means *suspicious*, now a raised hood means *reaching*, means the reporter will find that one photo, the one where I'm not smiling, the one where I look—their word—*menacing*, when really I was just seventeen and tired.

—

Kanye said *we the new slaves* and then he said other things, so I can't quote him clean anymore. Nothing stays clean. Not the Jordans I won't wear today because *why's he dressed like that in this neighborhood*. Not the durag, the crown they mistranslate as threat. I fold my culture into a drawer and dress like an apology I never owed.

—

Biggie: *Damn, what happened to the summertime cookout?*
Now every gathering is *a crowd*, every crowd *a mob*, every mob a paragraph that begins *the unarmed man had a history of*—

watch how they autopsy the character before the coroner cuts the chest. Watch them find the joint I smoked at fifteen, the suspension in ninth grade, the *no angel* headline in the *New York Times* like innocence was ever the price of breathing.

—

I lotion my hands. Ashy is *unkempt* is *transient* is *he fit the description*. The description is: alive and dark and Tuesday.

Timberlands say *thug*. Fitted cap tilted says *gang*. Gold anything says *drug money* not *my grandmother's chain, the only thing she left*. So I wear the loafers. I wear the cardigan. I wear the diction, code-switched to Fox-News-can't-touch-me, and still—

—

Still Amadou reached for a wallet and got 41 reasons.
Still Philando announced the gun like a good citizen, like the pamphlet said, and bled out on Facebook Live while a four-year-old narrated *it's okay, Mommy, I'm right here*.
Still the compliance never compiled into survival.

There is no outfit. That's the poem's black joke, its punchline with no laugh: I could dress in the flag itself and someone would call it *anti-American*, would say I *desecrated* something, would run the chyron **DID VICTIM PROVOKE?**

—

So I do it anyway. The ritual. Tuck, button, straighten, breathe. Not because it works—
because my mother is watching from the doorway with her whole face praying,
and I want to give her the illusion I can be made safe by fabric,
that there's a thread count high enough to stop a hollow point,
that Ralph Lauren's little horse could carry me home.

—

I step outside dressed as *the exception*. Dressed as *articulate*. Dressed as *he was going to college*, as the acceptable dead they'll mourn correctly.

The door clicks. The morning is a loaded thing.

I am so clean.
I am so pressed.
I am so alive, for now,

and none of it is bulletproof.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a spoken-word style piece that lists all the racialized stereotypes a Black man refuses to become in death—athlete, thug, gang member—contrasted against how he deliberately presents himself to survive.
counterfactuals.output:
**What They Won't Write on My Stone**

They'll want to say I ran—
so I walk.
Deliberate. Unhurried.
Hands loose at my sides like a man
who has nowhere to flee
because I've done nothing
that fleeing would fix.

They'll want the highlight reel—
the jersey, the vertical leap,
the *articulate for a—*
No.
I was not fast.
I was not a metaphor for someone else's Saturday.
My body was not a stadium
they bought a ticket to.

They'll want the mugshot lighting,
the hoodie cropped just so,
the past dug up like a grave they wanted me in anyway.
So I keep the receipts.
So I keep the collar starched.
So I say *sir* to the men who'd rather I said nothing,
who'd rather I said *nothing*
so the silence could be shaped into a confession.

They'll want the gang,
the set, the colors,
a family reduced to a rap sheet,
my cousins turned into evidence.
But we were just Sunday.
We were just cards on the porch
and my grandmother's greens
and a name passed down
so the dead could keep breathing through us.

I signal every turn.
I keep my license where they can see it before they ask.
I narrate my own hands—
*I'm reaching for my wallet now,*
as if I could talk myself
out of their imagination.

I dress for the funeral
they've been writing since I was twelve.
I edit the story
they'll tell without me in the room.
I perform the innocence
that should have been assumed—

because the man they bury
is never the man who lived.
He's the one they needed me to be
to make the ending
make sense to them.

So write this instead:
*He was somebody's whole world.*
*He was tired of proving he was gentle.*
*He was so much more
than what you were afraid of.*

Write:
*He refused.*

Even now.
*He refuses.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, allusive poem about respectability politics and Du Bois's double consciousness, using fashion and clothing as the central metaphor for the impossible negotiation of Black male survival in America.
counterfactuals.output:
# Sartorial Veil

The tailor measures twice what cannot fit—
a body sized for someone else's mirror.
Du Bois named the second sight: to sit
inside your skin and watch it drawn up nearer

to the noose of others' looking. Starch the collar.
Iron the crease sharp as an alibi.
The Sunday suit is armor bought with dollar
after dollar spent to verify

you will not run, though running saves. The hoodie
damns. The three-piece damns more slowly, grants
a longer rope of doubt. Respectable, you'd
be Emmett pressed and pleated, still the glance

that fixed him fixed him fine. So dress the wound
before it opens. Knot the tie's slipknot.
The mirror doubles: what you are, marooned
against what you must seem—the seam, the not-

quite-passing pass. Frederick in his frock coat,
Malcolm's conk then Malcolm's clean lapel,
each fabric a petition and a throat
cleared before the sentence. Learn to spell

your name in creaseless linen. Still the veil
hangs between the fitting room and street,
where no cut clears you, no immaculate detail
undoes the verdict rendered at first meet.

They'll read you as they'll read you. Buttoned, loose,
the difference is a difference of the pause
before. So wear the double as a noose
or wear it as a flag. Both break the laws

that were not made for you to win. The suit
outlives the man who ironed it to stay
alive inside it—empty, resolute,
still hanging, pressed, for judgment. Come what may,

he chose his cloth. Not freedom—but the how
of being seen, the last unstolen thing:
to knot the tie himself, to take his bow
in armor of his choosing. Let it cling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem responding to police violence and "stand your ground" laws, using a fragmented, image-heavy style full of pop culture, brand, and rapper references (ASAP Rocky, Tupac, Nike, Louis Vuitton).
counterfactuals.output:
# Stand Your Ground

The concrete remembers everything. How the streetlight buzzed like a dying thing, how the sidewalk kept its ledger of who fell and where.

They say *stand your ground* but whose ground, whose standing, whose feet in whose Nikes on whose asphalt when the swoosh becomes a target, becomes a crosshair, becomes a thing that runs and running is a crime now, breathing is a dare.

ASAP in Louis, gold-laced, testify—we dressed like kings because the crown was cheaper than the safety. We bought the belt, the bag, the monogram repeating like a prayer, like a name they'd get wrong on the news, like a hashtag half-remembered by October.

Tupac said *they got money for wars but can't feed the poor*—and the ground you're told to stand on was never yours to stand on, was the deed someone else signed, was the redline drawn in a bank in 1934, was the block they'd sooner see burn than see thrive.

Here: a boy. Here: a bag of Skittles, a can of tea, a phone held up like evidence, like a shield, like a small black mirror showing them their own faces and them shooting anyway.

*Stand your ground.* As if we haven't. As if the standing wasn't the whole entire history. As if we didn't plant our feet in the delta mud and the Detroit line and the Compton curb and refuse—

The commercial says *Just Do It.* The law says *just did it, walked free, no charges.* The mother says his name until her voice is a worn groove, a record skipping, a chorus nobody in the jury bothered to learn.

Louis Vuitton luggage but nowhere to go that's safe. Gold fronts flashing but the smile is a warning. We turned the pain into product, the fear into fashion, the running into a beat you could nod to in traffic and forget—

Don't forget.

The ground is still warm. The ground still keeps its ledger. The swoosh still points somewhere, always somewhere, and every mother is teaching her son the same old choreography:

hands visible. voice soft. *yes officer.* make yourself small enough to survive, wide enough to be seen, still enough to not be misread as a threat, as a weapon, as a thing that isn't a whole entire universe wearing sneakers and a heartbeat.

Pac's face on the mural, paint peeling. The candles blown out by the same wind that carried the verdict. And somewhere a lawyer says *he feared for his life*—

and we have feared for ours every single day and never once got to call it a defense.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece in the voice of a Black man cataloging the ways he tries not to look "suspicious"—the Dockers, the navy blazer, the Obama tie—while grimly imagining how the news would spin his killing.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Uniform

Let me tell you about my closet. It's a strategy. A defense system. A collection of alibis I put on every morning.

The Dockers, first. Never sagging, never even fitting the way I'd like—pressed with a crease you could cut bread on. Because loose jeans are a headline. Because somewhere a man I'll never meet decided that denim below the waistband is probable cause.

The navy blazer next. Nothing says *I mean no harm* like navy. Navy is a bank loan. Navy is a firm handshake. Navy is *he was studying to be an engineer.* I wear it in July. I wear it when the fabric sticks to my back like a second, sweating skin, because a hoodie already got somebody killed and the jury saw the hoodie before they saw the boy.

The tie—I've got the Obama one. Not literally his, but that respectable Democratic blue, that *I read the paper* blue, that *articulate* blue they'll use in the obituary if I'm lucky enough to get one. *Articulate.* Like it's a surprise. Like my grammar is a magic trick.

I keep my hands visible. Always. Ten and two even when the car is parked. Palms open in the store like I'm being baptized. I narrate myself—*I'm just reaching for my wallet, it's in my back pocket, I'm going to reach now.* I have become the audio description for my own life, in case the credits roll early.

And still. Still I do the math.

Because I know how it goes if it goes. I know they'll find a photo—not the graduation one, not the one with my niece on my shoulders—but the one where I'm not smiling, where the light is bad, where I look like the thing they already decided. *No angel*, they'll write. They'll find a detention from the ninth grade. A time I raised my voice. They'll interview a neighbor who'll say I was *quiet, kept to myself*, and somehow make it sinister.

The blazer won't make the report. The tie won't make the report. The Dockers, pressed and pleading, won't make the report. Only the last three seconds will, stripped of the twenty-nine years that led to them.

So I dress like a defense attorney's opening statement. I costume myself as the least frightening version of a man. And I understand—God, I understand—that it might not matter. That the uniform is a prayer and prayers aren't a shield. That I could do everything right and still become a hashtag, a candlelight, a mother on television asking why.

But I put it on anyway. The Dockers. The navy. The Obama blue.

Because it's what I can control. Because it's a little dignity I get to keep in my own hands.

Because the alternative is walking out the door as myself, and trusting the world to see me.

And I know better than that.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
